Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control
I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
go along with whatever others want to feel safe

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette:
Ravi was 26 when he was taken captive during a contracting assignment in a conflict zone. He remembers the moment of capture as a single snapshot-the dust, the shouting, the cold metal of a gun barrel against his temple. For six weeks he was held in a windowless room. The memories come back as distinct pictures: the guard's boots, the crack in the ceiling, the taste of stale bread. Sometimes when he remembers, he feels the same crushing pain in his ribs where they kicked him. Other times, he recalls the events with a strange numbness, as if watching a stranger's life. Now, fifteen years later, he works as a park ranger. The job puts him alone on quiet trails, but also in contact with strangers-hikers, uniformed colleagues, visitors who sometimes talk about military service.

After his release, Ravi could not shake the feeling that he was permanently marked by what had happened. He felt humiliated-not only by what was done to him, but by his own perceived cowardice. He began to believe that somebody else, someone stronger, would never have allowed themselves to be captured. This sense of isolation grew. He withdrew from friends, certain they could not understand, and that their pity only confirmed his shame. One evening at a family gathering, his uncle's brother-a veteran-started talking about his time in the military. The words hit Ravi like a physical blow, and the snapshot of the guard's boots flashed into his mind with terrifying clarity. From then on, any talk of the military brought the memories rushing back, each snapshot more vivid than the last. Authority figures in uniform also became potent triggers. Even the friendly park ranger uniform he wore felt dangerous. When a hiker stopped him for directions, he would feel suddenly exposed, his heart racing, convinced they could see the humiliation written on his face. Because he felt so isolated, Ravi became hypervigilant to signs that others were watching or judging him, so every glance from a visitor seemed like a potential threat.

The hypervigilance fed directly into his threat response. At the sound of a sudden movement-a twig snapping behind him, a mountain biker rounding a corner too fast-he would flinch as if under attack, his body bracing for the next kick. These startle reactions often triggered the memory itself, the pain in his ribs returning. Even when his supervisor assured him the trails were safe, Ravi could not believe it. Safety felt like a lie. The flashbacks came without warning: for a few seconds he would be back in that room, freezing or dropping whatever he held. Each flashback convinced him that he was permanently damaged, that the humiliation was inescapable. After each flashback, he found himself scanning the environment for anything that might provoke another-the sound of a zipper, the shape of a uniformed figure in the distance-so that ordinary moments became charged with the possibility of danger. His belief that he was broken reinforced the memories, making him dwell on the most degrading moments of his captivity and bringing those snapshots to mind more often.

To regain some control, Ravi began to restrict his eating. The hunger felt familiar, almost comforting, because it was a choice. When the memory of the pain in his ribs surfaced, he would skip lunch, convinced that by controlling his body he could control the past. But the restriction also made him weak-it increased his startle response, leaving him shaky and more vulnerable to sudden noises. He also found himself lost in revenge fantasies, imagining hunting down the men who had held him. These fantasies kept the memory vivid and fresh, and they kept his nervous system on edge, making his startle reflex even more hair-trigger. The fantasies also made him hyperaware of any potential reminder of his captors-a man with a certain gait, a voice with a familiar accent-so that these ordinary things became triggers he could not ignore. At work, he fell into people pleasing: agreeing with every visitor, never asserting himself, doing whatever his colleagues asked to avoid any conflict. This only deepened his sense of humiliation, as he saw himself as a man who could not stand up for anything. His partner noticed his passivity and began to worry, but Ravi could not explain why he needed so badly to be liked.

The cycle tightened. Each startle response triggered another snapshot. Each memory reinforced his belief that he was broken and isolated. That belief made him even more vigilant for signs of threat, so a distant voice or a glimpse of a uniform could send him reeling. His revenge fantasies, meant to discharge anger, instead kept the perpetrators alive in his mind, making him more sensitive to any mention of the military. His people pleasing meant he never said no, so he was always in situations that felt unsafe. When he restricted eating, his physical sensations mimicked those of captivity, pulling him back into a snapshot of hunger and helplessness.

Ravi sought help because he could no longer function. His weight had dropped, and his partner had threatened to leave, exhausted by his emotional distance. At work, he had started to avoid certain trails where he might encounter uniformed colleagues. What frightened him most was the thought that he would never feel safe again, that the humiliation was now part of who he was. He wanted to believe it could change, but the self-comparison whispered that someone else would already have gotten past this.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory causes or leads to the activation of triggers; instead, triggers typically cause the memory.

No paragraph shows that maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, restraint, people pleasing) cause the occurrence or salience of triggers; instead, they usually lead to other outcomes like threat or memory.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory causes or leads to the activation of triggers; instead, triggers typically cause the memory.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph shows that maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, restraint, people pleasing) cause the occurrence or salience of triggers; instead, they usually lead to other outcomes like threat or memory.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
